title: AI No Get Enemy
author: Charlie Barone
summary: Charlie Barone uses Fela Kuti's song "Water No Get Enemy" as a metaphor for AI in education: some things become so woven into daily life that being against them stops being a real position, and the question becomes how rather than whether. He grants the real harms, including lost jobs, unthought essays, deepfakes and chatbot-related harm to children, but argues that many in education remain in an anti-water stage of bans and pen-and-paper fixes. New NPU polling of more than 1,500 K-12 parents shows strong support for teaching AI safety and effective use, with limits preferred over bans by about seven to one, and a Learning Heroes poll shows similar comfort. He argues that children who never learn to swim are most likely to drown, so schools should teach students to question and check tools. He warns that later technologies such as brain implants and gene editing will raise harder questions, and that the habits built now must include honest risk talk and asking who benefits.
points: Barone argues that AI, like water, is too embedded to be opposed as a category, so the useful question for schools is how to engage with it.
Parent polling shows no majority support for any classroom ban, with limits preferred to bans about seven to one and strong backing for teaching AI safety and use.
Pen-and-paper limits and phone confiscation are described as short-term fixes, while banned tools get used secretly and badly.
He warns that inevitability can be used as a weapon by powerful actors, so active engagement must include asking who profits and who is hurt.
He frames today's AI as a rehearsal for harder technologies such as brain implants and gene editing, which will test schools and society more.
quotes: Fela isn't telling you water is gentle, or that the drowning was somehow for the best. He's saying water can take the most precious thing you have, and you still can't separate it from the rhythms of daily life.
But Fela's point still holds: some things become so woven into how we live that being "against" them stops being a real position. At that point the question isn't whether, but how.

I can see some value in, for example, as some suggest, limiting student classwork and exams to pen and paper, students spending less time on their Chromebooks, or confiscating student phones at the beginning of the school day. But those solutions are short-term and shortsighted.

In a survey of more than 1,500 parents of K-12 public school students, 85% of parents support K-12 public schools teaching students about AI safety; 77% support K-12 public schools teaching students ways to use AI tools effectively. No version of a classroom ban on AI or devices gets majority support.
When parents are asked to choose between banning a technology and setting limits on it, limits win by about seven to one.
A kid who has never learned to swim is the most likely to drown. The same goes for the kids for whom we try to ban AI: they'll use it anyway, in secret and badly.
Powerful people love to tell the rest of us that technology is inevitable, as if inevitability means you should stop asking who profits, who's hurt, and who decided.

The habits we build now will be the ones we rely on when the stakes get much higher: telling people honestly about the risks, building rules before the damage happens, teaching kids to question new tools and not just use them, and always asking who benefits.
